extracted.intended_audience: citizens and delegates deliberating the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of The Federalist Papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical arguments for structuring the chief executive's powers in the U.S. Constitution (veto, military command, pardons, treaties, appointments). Focuses on who should hold which powers and checks to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified negative (executive veto) preferred to absolute negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of an absolute negative, it is proposed to give the Executive the qualified negative already described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualified negative (returning a bill for reconsideration, subject to being finally rejected only if more than one third of each house concur in sufficiency of objections) is more readily exercised than an absolute veto. It offends less, encourages use, unites the Executive with a respectable portion of the legislature when opposition prevails, and has a silent restraining effect on unjustifiable pursuits by creating an external impediment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep judges distinct from executive revisionary functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The judges, who are to be the interpreters of the law, might receive an improper bias from having given a previous opinion in their revisionary capacities; by being often associated with the Executive they might be induced to embark too far in the political views of that magistrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is impossible to keep the judges too distinct from every other avocation than that of expounding the laws. Placing judges in a position to be corrupted or influenced by the Executive is peculiarly dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vest command of military and naval forces in a single Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The President of the United States is to be 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States when called into the actual service of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction of war demands the qualities of a single hand: direction of the common strength, decision and unity of command. Historically, state constitutions concentrate military authority in the chief magistrate; this is appropriate for effective conduct of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power vested in the President, broadly unfettered (except impeachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: He is also to be authorized to grant 'reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanity and good policy dictate that pardoning be as little fettered as possible; single executive responsibility fosters scrupulousness and caution in mercy. A single magistrate is more eligible to dispense mercy than a body of men, who may encourage each other to obduracy or to imprudent clemency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for treason and insurrections re: pardon
rubrics_metrics.description: The expediency of vesting the power of pardoning in the President has been contested in relation to the crime of treason; some urge legislative concurrence, but there are strong objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While legislative concurrence for treason has arguments (society-level offense; fear of executive connivance), practical objections include the danger that legislatures may be tainted by the same spirit as the offenders, or that delay (convening legislature) would forfeit critical opportunities to offer pardons in insurrections or rebellions when timeliness can restore tranquility. Delegating discretionary power beforehand is questionable and might embolden guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making by President with Senate advice and consent (two-thirds of senators present)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties are contracts between sovereigns that have the force of law but derive from good faith; their nature is distinct from purely legislative or executive functions. Joint possession by the Executive and a portion of the legislature (Senate) combines the Executive's suitability for negotiation with legislative participation due to treaties' lawlike effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making belongs with Senate (not House) because of required qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Representatives should not be associated in treaty-making because its fluctuating and multitudinous composition forbids expectation of those qualities essential to the trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty-making demands accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics, steady adherence to views, sensibility to national character, decision, secrecy, and despatch—qualities incompatible with a numerous, frequently changing body like the House. Including the House would introduce complexity, expense, and delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two-thirds of senators present (not two-thirds of whole body) to approve treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision requires two thirds of the senators present to concur, rather than two thirds of all members composing the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring a fixed proportion of the whole body tends toward paralysis (near unanimity when absences occur) and diminishes motive for punctual attendance. A proportion of attending members promotes punctuality, keeps the body complete, reduces delays, and better secures the advantages of a numerous agency without excessive obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid demanding supermajority thresholds beyond necessary majority for government operations
rubrics_metrics.description: All provisions which require more than the majority of any body to its resolutions have a tendency to embarrass government operations and subject the majority's sense to that of the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive supermajorities historically produce impotence and perplexity (Roman Tribuneship, Polish Diet, States-General examples). The convention balanced security with activity by not requiring unreasonably large majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointments: President nominates; Senate advises and consents
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is 'to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, ... judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers ... whose appointments are not otherwise provided for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomination vests primary judgment in the President while Senate concurrence serves as a check against favoritism. Nomination produces responsibility without the evils of absolute appointment power, and the Senate's role encourages careful selection and stability in administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single nominator (President) is preferable to a collective appointing body
rubrics_metrics.description: One man of discernment is better fitted to analyze and estimate the peculiar qualities adapted to particular offices than a body of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single responsible person will have fewer personal attachments and be less distracted by diverse private interests than an assembly; undivided responsibility creates a livelier sense of duty and careful investigation of candidates' qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate concurrence acts as a salutary check and source of administrative stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of the Senate's concurrence would have a powerful, though generally silent, operation: an excellent check upon favoritism and an efficacious source of stability in the administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possibility of rejection motivates care in nominations; the Senate restrains appointments made from state prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or view to popularity. It also prevents wholesale displacement of officers after a change in President, as the Senate's approval is necessary to remove as well as appoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointments to fill vacancies temporarily
rubrics_metrics.description: The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision allows temporary continuity of administration when the Senate is not in session; commissions expire at the end of the next Senate session, preserving the Senate's ultimate confirmation role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against conflicts of interest in appointments (eligibility restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No senator or representative shall during the time for which he was elected, be appointed to any civil office under the United States which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person holding any office under the United States, shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constitutional restrictions are provided to prevent appointments motivated by self-interest or corrupt bargains between legislative and executive branches, and to reduce executive influence over the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid secret small appointment councils; prefer public nomination and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing the federal plan with the State constitution's council of appointment (small body, private, impenetrable to public eye), the federal mode (President's nomination + Senate's public concurrence) is to be preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret councils allow cabal and intrigue, obscure responsibility, diminish public accountability, and produce improper appointments. Public modes expose actions to the public, so blame and praise attach clearly to actors (President for nomination; Senate for approval or rejection).
